docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the port. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SLAS605 C: Supplies, reference and SCLK limits: 7.3 Recommended Operating Conditions, p. 10 Serial timing, CS high time and the 16-clock frame: 7.9 Timing Requirements; Figures 1 and 2, p. 17 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on a class you derive from ads7952::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/ads7952_spi_interface.hpp ). The base uses CRTP and declares no hook itself; the driver template is constrained by the ads7952::SpiPort concept, so calls are resolved at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error at the point of use. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the bus up on the first call; return true at once afterwards. false makes the driver's EnsureInitialized() return Bus bool Transfer(const uint8_t* tx, uint8_t* rx, std::size_t len) noexcept yes One 16-bit frame: len is always 2 and both buffers are set; CS low for both bytes and high after. false on any bus error void DelayUs(uint32_t us) noexcept yes Wait at least us microseconds; used once, for the power-up time after the start-up reset void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) noexcept no Print one line; message is plain text, never a format string The port ¶ my_port.hpp class MyPort : public ads7952 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_spi_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One 16-bit frame: CS low for both bytes, high after. The driver always passes len = 2. bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds: used once, for the power-up time after the reset. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the transfer must follow: One call, one frame. Keep CS low for exactly the 16 clocks of the 2 bytes and raise it after: the chip samples its input and starts a conversion on every CS falling edge, so CS must toggle between frames (at least 20 ns high, section 7.9). A port that bursts several frames under one CS breaks the chip's frame count. The bus requirements below : mode 0, MSB first, up to kMaxClockHz (20 MHz), the 16 clocks of a frame back to back (8-bit words with no idle clock between the two bytes, or one 16-bit word). Start at 1 MHz on jumper wires. Mind the acquisition time. The next channel acquires from the 14 th clock of a frame to the next CS falling edge (section 8.1). A faster clock and back-to-back frames shorten it; pick the rate for your input network (a board running SPI at 4 MHz with software-timed frames sees gaps of tens of microseconds). Raw bytes only. Do not interpret, retry or reorder bytes; the driver owns the framing and the retries. Return false for a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus and never ignores it. A port that cannot report a failure would turn every failed transfer into a frame of data; a void Transfer() is a compile error. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever. Bus requirements ¶ The driver states what the ADS795x needs from the bus as constexpr values in inc/ads7952_spi_interface.hpp (handbook KB-CPP-123). Check your port's settings against them with static_assert , as both example ports do, so a port that clocks too fast or in the wrong mode does not compile. The values hold for every +VBD from 1.7 V to 5.25 V (the largest minimum of section 7.9 is taken): Constant Value Meaning (datasheet) kSpiMode 0 CPOL 0, CPHA 0: SDI latched on the rising edge, SDO changes on the falling edge (8.1, Figure 2) kMsbFirst true DI15 and DO15 first (Figure 2) kMaxClockHz 20'000'000 f(SCLK) max (7.3, 7.9) kMinCsHighNs 20 CS high between two frames, t_w1 (7.9) kCsSetupNs 8 CS low to the first rising SCLK edge, t_su1 at +VBD = 1.8 V (7.9) kCsHoldNs 0 7.9 gives no minimum: CS may rise once the 16 th SCLK falling edge has passed (8.1) kQuietNs , kSdoReleaseNs 40 , 26 SDO 3-state to the next CS falling edge, t_q; the 16 th SCLK falling edge to SDO 3-state, t_d3 (7.9). The 16 th falling edge comes at least 66 ns before the next CS falling edge kContinuousWord true No idle SCLK between the two bytes: the chip converts with SCLK (t_conv = 16 SCLK) and the datasheet does not specify a conversion with the clock stopped kFrameBits 16 One frame is one 16-bit word with CS low throughout (8.1) Control pins ¶ The ADS795x has no reset, enable or other control input: its only control line is CS, and the port (or the SPI peripheral) owns it. CS idles high. Drive it high before its output is enabled and before the first frame, so the chip sees no CS falling edge it was not sent (handbook KB-HW-018); the ESP32 port does this before spi_bus_add_device() , and a pull-up on CS keeps it high while the MCU resets. GPIO0 to GPIO3 are inputs after a reset (Table 11) and the driver sets them from Config::gpio ; the driver has no GpioSet() hook. Optional hooks ¶ The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with named concepts in one place ( ads7952::detail : HasDelayUs , HasLog ), which check the exact signature, noexcept and the result type. A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way or fails to compile; a hook that is declared with another signature ( DelayUs(uint16_t) , a Log without noexcept ) is a compile error, never skipped silently. Hook Used for Without it DelayUs() The power-up time ( kPowerUpUs , 1 µs) after the start-up reset Compile error at EnsureInitialized() Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with every hook: class FullPort : public ads7952 :: SpiInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_spi_init (); } // One 16-bit frame per call: CS low for both bytes, high after (the chip converts on each CS // falling edge). bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Required: the power-up time after the reset in EnsureInitialized(). void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( ads7952 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > ads7952 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } }; The required hooks are checked as exactly: a Transfer() that returns void , takes a narrower length ( uint16_t len ) or is not noexcept does not satisfy SpiPort (handbook KB-CPP20-006), so it is a compile error instead of a silent truncation. The compile-fail tests check each case, and the missing DelayUs() . Reference implementations ¶ Every port lives with its example, in examples/<platform>/ ; the driver has none. Platforms lists them and how to add one. examples/host/host_ads7952_port.hpp : any PC, against a simulated chip. Start from it for a host build or a test bench; it is also the smallest complete port. examples/esp32/main/esp32_ads7952_port.hpp : ESP-IDF, with every hook. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Check your port ¶ Build it: the ports on this page are compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over them. Call EnsureInitialized() : Ok proves that SDI reaches the chip and SDO comes back, frame by frame (the identity check reads back the channel addresses it selects). Call TraceFrames(ch, words) with a channel wired to a known voltage: from words[2] on the address is ch and the code matches the voltage ( ToMicrovolts() ). Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several chips share a bus, the port must also serialise the bus. See Contract . Editor setup ¶ The clang-format and clang-tidy configuration is in _config/ , and the repository root has no copy of it. Tools that take a path use it directly; CI does the same: Tool Setting Command line clang-format --style=file:_config/.clang-format , clang-tidy --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy -p build VS Code (C/C++ extension) "C_Cpp.clang_format_style": "file:${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-format" and "C_Cpp.codeAnalysis.clangTidy.args": ["--config-file=${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-tidy"] clangd (VS Code clangd, Neovim, Emacs), CLion These find .clang-format and .clang-tidy only by name, from the file upwards: copy both to the root once ( cp _config/.clang-format _config/.clang-tidy . ). .gitignore lists the copies, so they never reach a commit; copy again after _config/ changes Configure with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (clangd: --compile-commands-dir=build ) so the editor sees the same flags as the build.

The values hold for every +VBD from 1.7 V to 5.25 V (the largest minimum of section 7.9 is taken): Constant Value Meaning (datasheet) kSpiMode 0 CPOL 0, CPHA 0: SDI latched on the rising edge, SDO changes on the falling edge (8.1, Figure 2) kMsbFirst true DI15 and DO15 first (Figure 2) kMaxClockHz 20'000'000 f(SCLK) max (7.3, 7.9) kMinCsHighNs 20 CS high between two frames, t_w1 (7.9) kCsSetupNs 8 CS low to the first rising SCLK edge, t_su1 at +VBD = 1.8 V (7.9) kCsHoldNs 0 7.9 gives no minimum: CS may rise once the 16 th SCLK falling edge has passed (8.1) kQuietNs , kSdoReleaseNs 40 , 26 SDO 3-state to the next CS falling edge, t_q; the 16 th SCLK falling edge to SDO 3-state, t_d3 (7.9). The 16 th falling edge comes at least 66 ns before the next CS falling edge kContinuousWord true No idle SCLK between the two bytes: the chip converts with SCLK (t_conv = 16 SCLK) and the datasheet does not specify a conversion with the clock stopped kFrameBits 16 One frame is one 16-bit word with CS low throughout (8.1)

docs.text: The ADS795x has no reset, enable or other control input: its only control line is CS, and the port (or the SPI peripheral) owns it. CS idles high. Drive it high before its output is enabled and before the first frame, so the chip sees no CS falling edge it was not sent (handbook KB-HW-018); the ESP32 port does this before spi_bus_add_device() , and a pull-up on CS keeps it high while the MCU resets. GPIO0 to GPIO3 are inputs after a reset (Table 11) and the driver sets them from Config::gpio ; the driver has no GpioSet() hook.
docs.title: Control pins

docs.text: The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with named concepts in one place ( ads7952::detail : HasDelayUs , HasLog ), which check the exact signature, noexcept and the result type. A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way or fails to compile; a hook that is declared with another signature ( DelayUs(uint16_t) , a Log without noexcept ) is a compile error, never skipped silently. Hook Used for Without it DelayUs() The power-up time ( kPowerUpUs , 1 µs) after the start-up reset Compile error at EnsureInitialized() Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with every hook: class FullPort : public ads7952 :: SpiInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_spi_init (); } // One 16-bit frame per call: CS low for both bytes, high after (the chip converts on each CS // falling edge). bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Required: the power-up time after the reset in EnsureInitialized(). void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( ads7952 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > ads7952 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } }; The required hooks are checked as exactly: a Transfer() that returns void , takes a narrower length ( uint16_t len ) or is not noexcept does not satisfy SpiPort (handbook KB-CPP20-006), so it is a compile error instead of a silent truncation. The compile-fail tests check each case, and the missing DelayUs() .

docs.text: The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several chips share a bus, the port must also serialise the bus. See Contract .

Try it on your PC ¶ examples/host/ runs the real driver against a simulated ADS7952, through a host port. From the repository root, with CMake and a C++20 compiler: cmake -S examples/host -B build-example cmake --build build-example ./build-example/ads7952_host_example ADS7952 driver 0.1.0 on the host ads7952: initialised CH3: 901 (549926 uV) CH0=163 CH1=409 CH2=655 CH3=901 CH6=1638 CH7=1884 CH9=2375 CH11=2867 CH0=163 CH1=409 CH2=655 CH3=901 CH6=1638 CH7=1884 CH9=2375 CH11=2867 The calls in main.cpp are the ones below; only the port differs on an MCU. CI builds and runs this example on every pull request. 1. Wire it ¶ MCU ADS7952 (TSSOP-38) Notes SPI SCLK SCLK (pin 32) Mode 0, up to 20 MHz; 1 MHz for bring-up on jumper wires SPI MOSI SDI (pin 33) SPI MISO SDO (pin 34) High impedance while CS is high, so the bus can be shared GPIO or hardware CS CS (pin 31) Low for one 16-bit frame, high between frames 1.7 V to +VA +VBD (pin 36) Digital I/O supply: the MCU's I/O voltage 2.7 V to 5.25 V +VA (pins 5, 29) Analog supply, decoupled at the pins 2.5 V reference REFP, REFM (pins 4, 3) 10 µF between them MXO to AINP (pins 7, 8), AINM (9) to ground Directly, or through a buffer The GPIOs can stay unconnected for this example (they reset as inputs). The Hardware page has the full pin list and the timing. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the ads7952::ads7952 CMake target. Installation covers CMake on any MCU, the installed package and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ads7952.git external/driver-ads7952 3. Write the port ¶ The port is the only platform code: it brings the bus up, moves one 16-bit frame per call and waits. Replace the platform_* calls with your SDK's. my_port.hpp class MyPort : public ads7952 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_spi_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One 16-bit frame: CS low for both bytes, high after. The driver always passes len = 2. bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds: used once, for the power-up time after the reset. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Porting explains each method, the optional hook and the transfer rules. 4. Read a channel ¶ main.cpp #include "ads7952.hpp" int read_input_3 ( MyPort & port , uint32_t & microvolts ) { ads7952 :: ADS7952 < MyPort > adc ( port ); // no I/O yet; Config{} is an ADS7952 at its reset state if ( auto r = adc . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. bus up, reset, registers, identity check return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus, NoDevice or DeviceIdMismatch: check wiring } const auto code = adc . ReadChannel ( 3 ); // 2. Manual mode: select, acquire, convert if ( ! code ) { return static_cast < int > ( code . error ); // ChannelMismatch: a reply for another channel } microvolts = adc . ToMicrovolts ( code . value ); // 3. 0 to VREF, one LSB = VREF / 4096 return 0 ; } What each step does: EnsureInitialized() calls your port's EnsureInitialized() , resets the chip through its GPIO program register, writes Config{} (the reset values: Range 1, every channel in Auto-1) and checks that the replies carry the channel addresses it selects: a wiring fault fails here, not later. ReadChannel(3) selects channel 3 in Manual mode and returns its result two frames later, after checking that the reply carries address 3. Reading channel 3 again costs one frame. ToMicrovolts() converts the 12-bit code with the configured range and reference. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. docs.text: Reference, range and supplies ¶ How a code becomes a voltage, which voltages set that scale, how to choose the range for a board, how the driver proves the scale at run time, and how to power and lay out the chip. Read this before you design a board or write the code that turns codes into engineering units: a wrong scale passes every address check the driver makes. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SLAS605 C: Absolute limits of the inputs and supplies: 7.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings, p. 10 Supplies, reference and SCLK limits: 7.3 Recommended Operating Conditions, p. 10 Input ranges, power-up time and the invalid first conversion: 7.6 Electrical Characteristics (ADS7950 to ADS7953), p. 12 The external reference and its 10 µF capacitor: 8.3.1 Reference, p. 29 Output codes and the LSB size: 8.5.1 Digital Output, Table 8, p. 41 GPIO program register and the register reset: 8.5.2 GPIO Registers, Figure 58, Table 11, p. 42 Analog input, source impedance and MXO to AINP: 9.1.1 Analog Input, Figures 60 and 61, p. 46 Supply range, decoupling and +VA at or above +VBD: 10 Power Supply Recommendations, p. 51 Layout of grounds, supply and reference capacitors: 11.1 Layout Guidelines; 11.2 Layout Examples, Figures 69 and 70, p. 52 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Three voltages, three jobs ¶ Voltage Pin What it sets Config field VREF REFP (to REFM) The scale of every code: full scale is VREF in Range 1, 2 x VREF in Range 2 vref_mv +VA +VA The analog supply. It limits the inputs (never above +VA + 0.3 V) and decides whether Range 2 is specified va_min_mv +VBD +VBD The SPI and GPIO logic levels, 1.7 V to +VA none A fourth voltage belongs to your sensors, not to the chip: the excitation of a ratiometric sensor, whose output is a fraction of its own supply. It is often the +VA rail, but it is never the ADC's full scale. Ratiometric sensors shows how to decode against it. From a code to a voltage ¶ The result is 12 bits, straight binary, and one LSB is full scale / 4096 (Table 8): Range Full scale One LSB (VREF = 2.5 V) Code 2048 Code 4095 1 ( Range::Vref ) VREF 610.4 µV VREF / 2 = 1.25 V VREF - 1 LSB = 2.4994 V 2 ( Range::TwoVref ) 2 x VREF 1.2207 mV VREF = 2.50 V 2 x VREF - 1 LSB = 4.9988 V Divide by 4096 , not 4095: dividing by 4095 reads every voltage 0.024 % high. The driver's ToMicrovolts() and CodeToMicrovolts() use Table 8 and return the bottom of the code's step. The driver keeps the range with the result: ToMicrovolts(code) uses the range configured now. Every Bank carries Bank::range , the range its codes were converted in, and ToMicrovolts(bank, channel) uses it. A bank kept across SetRange() still converts correctly. With GPIO2 as the range input, Config::range is what you declare the pin to be; the driver cannot see the pin. Declare a scale monitor to check the declaration. Choosing the range ¶ Range 2 is specified only "while 2 x VREF <= +VA" (section 7.6): the full-scale input span and the absolute input range of Range 2 both carry that condition. Validate() therefore refuses Range 2 unless 2 x vref_mv <= va_min_mv , and va_min_mv is the lowest +VA the board guarantees: the regulator's minimum after its tolerance, ripple and load steps, not the nominal rail. Board Range Why Inputs up to about 2.5 V, any +VA from 2.7 V 1, VREF 2.5 V Twice the resolution of Range 2, no condition on +VA Inputs up to 5 V, +VA guaranteed >= 5.0 V (for example a 5.1 V rail at ±1.5 %) 2, VREF 2.5 V Specified; full scale 5.0 V Inputs up to about 4 V, +VA a 5 V rail at ±5 % (4.75 V minimum) 2, VREF 2.048 V 2 x 2.048 = 4.096 V <= 4.75 V. Full scale 4.096 V, one LSB exactly 1 mV. Footnote 6 of section 7.6: below 2.4 V the SNR is lower Inputs up to 5 V, +VA a nominal 5.0 V that can sag Change the board Range 2 with 2 x VREF above +VA is outside the datasheet, and inputs near 5 V exceed +VA + 0.3 V when the rail sags Two rules hold in every range: No input above +VA + 0.3 V or below -0.3 V , at any time, powered or not (section 7.1). A sensor powered from another rail can drive an input while +VA is off; power them from the same rail or clamp the inputs. The range does not survive a reset. The chip powers up and resets in Range 1 (section 8.4.3, Table 1). The driver resets the chip in EnsureInitialized() and sends the range in every mode word it writes, the read frame of ReadChannel() included, but a brown-out between two calls puts the chip back in Range 1 without a flag. A reply from channel 0 out of turn shows it ( DeviceReset ); while the driver reads channel 0 alone only the monitor can, and CheckScale() then returns DeviceReset . Proving the scale: the scale monitor ¶ The chip has no register to read its range or its reference back. What the driver can check for free, the channel address of every reply, does not change with the range: a chip that lost its range returns perfectly addressed codes that are twice (or half) what they should be. The address nibble (DO15:12, section 8.1) does not depend on the range, and one LSB is VREF / 4096 in Range 1 against 2 x VREF / 4096 in Range 2 (Table 8): a chip back in Range 1 reads an input below VREF at twice its code, with every reply address valid. The only witness is a known input. Wire one channel to a voltage derived from REFP and declare it in Config::monitor : // A 5 V sensor board: a 2.5 V reference on REFP, and REFP also wired to channel 11. ads7952 :: Config SensorBoardConfig () { ads7952 :: Config c {}; c . range = ads7952 :: Range :: TwoVref ; // full scale 2 x 2.5 V = 5.0 V, one LSB = 1.22 mV c . vref_mv = 2500 ; // the reference's nominal value c . va_min_mv = 5000 ; // the lowest +VA the rail guarantees: 2 x 2500 <= 5000 c . auto1_channels = 0x0FFF ; // the scan includes the monitor channel // REFP on channel 11 reads 2048 in Range 2 and 4095 in Range 1: a lost range cannot pass. c . monitor = {. channel = 11 , . expected_uv = 2500000U , . tolerance_uv = 100000U }; // 2.5 V +/- 100 mV return c ; } Monitor input Range 1 code Range 2 code Notes REFP itself 4095 (clipped) 2048 Works for Range 2 only: in Range 1 it sits at full scale, where a clipped input also sits. Validate() refuses it in Range 1 REFP / 2, two equal resistors 2048 1024 Works in both ranges. Use 0.1 % resistors of the same series A voltage derived from REFP converts to the same code whatever REFP's exact value, so the check does not depend on the reference's accuracy. A monitor that is not derived from REFP also works, but its window must then absorb the reference's tolerance too. Validate() refuses a monitor that could not do its job: a channel the part lacks, a zero tolerance, a window that touches code 0 or 4095 (a dead or clipped input would pass), or windows of the two ranges that touch. Where What it checks Frames Result EnsureInitialized() Once, last, after the identity check 3 RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch ; the driver stays uninitialised CheckScale() On demand: the chip takes the range the driver sends, and REFP is there 1 to 3 The monitor's code, or the error CheckScaleCode(code) A code you already have: the monitor's entry of each Bank , or a DMA-decoded word 0 Ok , RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch RangeMismatch means the code is what the other range gives: GPIO2 is strapped to the other level, or the chip was reset. ScaleMismatch means neither range explains it: REFP is missing or not settled, or the monitor channel is not wired as declared. On the hot path, check the bank, not the chip. CheckScale() selects the monitor with a fresh mode word, which carries the range again, so it cannot see a range that was lost earlier and it costs frames. Put the monitor channel in the Auto-1 sequence and judge its code in every bank with CheckScaleCode() : the cost is one channel of the scan and no extra frame. // One scan, proved before any value leaves the driver layer. CheckScaleCode() costs no frame. ads7952 :: Error ReadProvedBank ( ads7952 :: ADS7952 < MyPort >& adc , ads7952 :: Bank & out ) { const auto bank = adc . ReadAuto1 (); if ( ! bank ) { return bank . error ; // DeviceReset / SequenceMismatch: the chip was reset; start it again } const ads7952 :: Error scale = adc . CheckScaleCode ( bank . value . code [ 11 ]); if ( scale != ads7952 :: Error :: Ok ) { return scale ; // RangeMismatch (x2 or /2) or ScaleMismatch (reference): do not publish } out = bank . value ; return ads7952 :: Error :: Ok ; } After a RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch , do not publish the bank. Restart with Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() : the reset and the start-up check run again. A failed CheckScale() leaves the driver uninitialised by itself. Ratiometric sensors ¶ A ratiometric sensor (for example a bridge or an amplified pressure sensor rated "10 % to 90 % of supply") outputs a fraction of its own supply . The ADC measures volts against VREF. Decoding the sensor against the ADC's full scale, or against a nominal 5.0 V, is only right while the sensor's supply is exactly that value. A supply that sags to 4.45 V while the decoder assumes 5.0 V under-reads every span by 11 % (4.45 / 5.0 = 0.89). Measure the sensor's supply on another channel of the same scan and divide: // A ratiometric sensor (output = a fraction of its own supply) read on channel 3, its supply // measured on channel 9 through a divider of exactly 1/2. Both conversions come from one bank, so // the reference and the range cancel: the result does not depend on VREF or on the 5 V rail. uint32_t SensorFractionPpm ( const ads7952 :: ADS7952 < MyPort >& adc , const ads7952 :: Bank & bank ) { const uint64_t signal_uv = adc . ToMicrovolts ( bank , 3 ); const uint64_t supply_uv = 2U * static_cast < uint64_t > ( adc . ToMicrovolts ( bank , 9 )); if ( supply_uv == 0U ) { return 0U ; // no supply: the caller treats the sensor as absent } return static_cast < uint32_t > (( signal_uv * 1000000U ) / supply_uv ); // 100000 = 10 % of supply } Choice Effect Supply measured in the same bank Reference and range cancel; supply ripple between the two conversions does not Divider for the supply channel Must keep the supply's channel inside the range: ½ puts a 5 V supply at 2.5 V No supply measurement The result is only as good as the rail's tolerance: say so where the value is used Power and layout ¶ From sections 8.3.1, 9.1.1, 10 and 11 of the datasheet: Item Requirement +VA 2.7 V to 5.25 V, well regulated; 1 µF ceramic at each +VA pin, as close as possible +VBD 1.7 V to +VA (never above +VA); 1 µF ceramic at the pin REFP An external low-noise reference (the datasheet names the REF5025, a 2.5 V band-gap); 10 µF ceramic from REFP to REFM, directly next to the pins, its ground routed to REFM by a short trace Characterised reference The electrical tables are measured at VREF = 2.5 V ± 0.1 V; section 8.3.1 asks for 2.5 V ± 10 mV; the chip operates from 2.0 V to 3.0 V Grounds A copper fill under the chip ties AGND, BDGND, AINM and REFM, with at least four vias to the analog ground plane Vias None between a decoupling capacitor and its pin Analog inputs With MXO tied to AINP, a source impedance of 50 Ω or less; a buffer between MXO and AINP relaxes it (Figure 61) Digital lines Kept apart from the analog inputs: the input bandwidth makes the chip sensitive to digital edges Inputs -0.3 V to +VA + 0.3 V, absolute (section 7.1) Design guidance that is not in the datasheet, to confirm on your bench: A resistor divider for the monitor or a supply channel has a high source impedance. Put a capacitor from the channel to AGND (for example 100 nF) so that the sample charge comes from it, and check that the reading does not move with the SCLK rate or the position of the channel in the sequence. Measure +VA at the chip under full load (the sensors on, motors and other loads running) before choosing the range. The value to declare is the lowest you saw, less the regulator's tolerance. Checklist for a new board ¶ Choose VREF and the range from the table in Choosing the range ; write vref_mv and the worst-case va_min_mv . Wire a scale monitor (REFP, or REFP / 2 for Range 1) to a spare channel and declare Config::monitor . Put the monitor channel in the Auto-1 sequence and check its code in every bank. Decode ratiometric sensors against their measured supply, never against the ADC's full scale. Convert with ToMicrovolts(bank, channel) , so a code is always converted with the range it was made in. On the bench: start with GPIO2 strapped wrong (if you use it) and with REFP disconnected; EnsureInitialized() must return RangeMismatch and ScaleMismatch . Worked example: a 5 V sensor board ¶ A board with ratiometric 5 V sensors, +VA from a nominal 5 V rail and a 2.5 V reference in Range 2: Check Range 2 against the lowest +VA. Range 2 needs 2 x VREF <= +VA (section 7.6). With +VA measured at 4.89 V to 4.91 V under load, below 2 x VREF = 5.0 V, Validate() refuses va_min_mv = 4890. Either raise and tighten +VA, or move to a 2.048 V reference (full scale 4.096 V; VREF may be 2 V to 3 V, section 7.3), and decide it with the sensor span in hand. Declare the monitor channel from the schematic. With channel 11 wired to REFP itself, the scale monitor is {11, 2500000, 100000} and reads 2048 in Range 2. A divided monitor (REFP through a resistor divider) needs the divided voltage instead, so read the schematic before declaring it. Divide by 4096. One LSB is full scale / 4096 (Table 8); a division by 4095 reads 0.024 % high. Decode the sensors against a measured excitation , taken from the same bank where you can ( Ratiometric sensors ). docs.text: How a code becomes a voltage, which voltages set that scale, how to choose the range for a board, how the driver proves the scale at run time, and how to power and lay out the chip. Read this before you design a board or write the code that turns codes into engineering units: a wrong scale passes every address check the driver makes. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SLAS605 C: Absolute limits of the inputs and supplies: 7.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings, p. 10 Supplies, reference and SCLK limits: 7.3 Recommended Operating Conditions, p. 10 Input ranges, power-up time and the invalid first conversion: 7.6 Electrical Characteristics (ADS7950 to ADS7953), p. 12 The external reference and its 10 µF capacitor: 8.3.1 Reference, p. 29 Output codes and the LSB size: 8.5.1 Digital Output, Table 8, p. 41 GPIO program register and the register reset: 8.5.2 GPIO Registers, Figure 58, Table 11, p. 42 Analog input, source impedance and MXO to AINP: 9.1.1 Analog Input, Figures 60 and 61, p. 46 Supply range, decoupling and +VA at or above +VBD: 10 Power Supply Recommendations, p. 51 Layout of grounds, supply and reference capacitors: 11.1 Layout Guidelines; 11.2 Layout Examples, Figures 69 and 70, p. 52 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map .

docs.text: Voltage Pin What it sets Config field VREF REFP (to REFM) The scale of every code: full scale is VREF in Range 1, 2 x VREF in Range 2 vref_mv +VA +VA The analog supply. It limits the inputs (never above +VA + 0.3 V) and decides whether Range 2 is specified va_min_mv +VBD +VBD The SPI and GPIO logic levels, 1.7 V to +VA none A fourth voltage belongs to your sensors, not to the chip: the excitation of a ratiometric sensor, whose output is a fraction of its own supply. It is often the +VA rail, but it is never the ADC's full scale. Ratiometric sensors shows how to decode against it.

docs.text: The result is 12 bits, straight binary, and one LSB is full scale / 4096 (Table 8): Range Full scale One LSB (VREF = 2.5 V) Code 2048 Code 4095 1 ( Range::Vref ) VREF 610.4 µV VREF / 2 = 1.25 V VREF - 1 LSB = 2.4994 V 2 ( Range::TwoVref ) 2 x VREF 1.2207 mV VREF = 2.50 V 2 x VREF - 1 LSB = 4.9988 V Divide by 4096 , not 4095: dividing by 4095 reads every voltage 0.024 % high. The driver's ToMicrovolts() and CodeToMicrovolts() use Table 8 and return the bottom of the code's step. The driver keeps the range with the result: ToMicrovolts(code) uses the range configured now. Every Bank carries Bank::range , the range its codes were converted in, and ToMicrovolts(bank, channel) uses it. A bank kept across SetRange() still converts correctly. With GPIO2 as the range input, Config::range is what you declare the pin to be; the driver cannot see the pin. Declare a scale monitor to check the declaration.
docs.title: From a code to a voltage

docs.text: Range 2 is specified only "while 2 x VREF <= +VA" (section 7.6): the full-scale input span and the absolute input range of Range 2 both carry that condition. Validate() therefore refuses Range 2 unless 2 x vref_mv <= va_min_mv , and va_min_mv is the lowest +VA the board guarantees: the regulator's minimum after its tolerance, ripple and load steps, not the nominal rail. Board Range Why Inputs up to about 2.5 V, any +VA from 2.7 V 1, VREF 2.5 V Twice the resolution of Range 2, no condition on +VA Inputs up to 5 V, +VA guaranteed >= 5.0 V (for example a 5.1 V rail at ±1.5 %) 2, VREF 2.5 V Specified; full scale 5.0 V Inputs up to about 4 V, +VA a 5 V rail at ±5 % (4.75 V minimum) 2, VREF 2.048 V 2 x 2.048 = 4.096 V <= 4.75 V. Full scale 4.096 V, one LSB exactly 1 mV. Footnote 6 of section 7.6: below 2.4 V the SNR is lower Inputs up to 5 V, +VA a nominal 5.0 V that can sag Change the board Range 2 with 2 x VREF above +VA is outside the datasheet, and inputs near 5 V exceed +VA + 0.3 V when the rail sags Two rules hold in every range: No input above +VA + 0.3 V or below -0.3 V , at any time, powered or not (section 7.1). A sensor powered from another rail can drive an input while +VA is off; power them from the same rail or clamp the inputs. The range does not survive a reset. The chip powers up and resets in Range 1 (section 8.4.3, Table 1). The driver resets the chip in EnsureInitialized() and sends the range in every mode word it writes, the read frame of ReadChannel() included, but a brown-out between two calls puts the chip back in Range 1 without a flag. A reply from channel 0 out of turn shows it ( DeviceReset ); while the driver reads channel 0 alone only the monitor can, and CheckScale() then returns DeviceReset .
docs.title: Choosing the range

docs.text: The chip has no register to read its range or its reference back. What the driver can check for free, the channel address of every reply, does not change with the range: a chip that lost its range returns perfectly addressed codes that are twice (or half) what they should be. The address nibble (DO15:12, section 8.1) does not depend on the range, and one LSB is VREF / 4096 in Range 1 against 2 x VREF / 4096 in Range 2 (Table 8): a chip back in Range 1 reads an input below VREF at twice its code, with every reply address valid. The only witness is a known input. Wire one channel to a voltage derived from REFP and declare it in Config::monitor : // A 5 V sensor board: a 2.5 V reference on REFP, and REFP also wired to channel 11. ads7952 :: Config SensorBoardConfig () { ads7952 :: Config c {}; c . range = ads7952 :: Range :: TwoVref ; // full scale 2 x 2.5 V = 5.0 V, one LSB = 1.22 mV c . vref_mv = 2500 ; // the reference's nominal value c . va_min_mv = 5000 ; // the lowest +VA the rail guarantees: 2 x 2500 <= 5000 c . auto1_channels = 0x0FFF ; // the scan includes the monitor channel // REFP on channel 11 reads 2048 in Range 2 and 4095 in Range 1: a lost range cannot pass. c . monitor = {. channel = 11 , . expected_uv = 2500000U , . tolerance_uv = 100000U }; // 2.5 V +/- 100 mV return c ; } Monitor input Range 1 code Range 2 code Notes REFP itself 4095 (clipped) 2048 Works for Range 2 only: in Range 1 it sits at full scale, where a clipped input also sits. Validate() refuses it in Range 1 REFP / 2, two equal resistors 2048 1024 Works in both ranges. Use 0.1 % resistors of the same series A voltage derived from REFP converts to the same code whatever REFP's exact value, so the check does not depend on the reference's accuracy. A monitor that is not derived from REFP also works, but its window must then absorb the reference's tolerance too. Validate() refuses a monitor that could not do its job: a channel the part lacks, a zero tolerance, a window that touches code 0 or 4095 (a dead or clipped input would pass), or windows of the two ranges that touch. Where What it checks Frames Result EnsureInitialized() Once, last, after the identity check 3 RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch ; the driver stays uninitialised CheckScale() On demand: the chip takes the range the driver sends, and REFP is there 1 to 3 The monitor's code, or the error CheckScaleCode(code) A code you already have: the monitor's entry of each Bank , or a DMA-decoded word 0 Ok , RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch RangeMismatch means the code is what the other range gives: GPIO2 is strapped to the other level, or the chip was reset. ScaleMismatch means neither range explains it: REFP is missing or not settled, or the monitor channel is not wired as declared. On the hot path, check the bank, not the chip. CheckScale() selects the monitor with a fresh mode word, which carries the range again, so it cannot see a range that was lost earlier and it costs frames. Put the monitor channel in the Auto-1 sequence and judge its code in every bank with CheckScaleCode() : the cost is one channel of the scan and no extra frame. // One scan, proved before any value leaves the driver layer. CheckScaleCode() costs no frame. ads7952 :: Error ReadProvedBank ( ads7952 :: ADS7952 < MyPort >& adc , ads7952 :: Bank & out ) { const auto bank = adc . ReadAuto1 (); if ( ! bank ) { return bank . error ; // DeviceReset / SequenceMismatch: the chip was reset; start it again } const ads7952 :: Error scale = adc . CheckScaleCode ( bank . value . code [ 11 ]); if ( scale != ads7952 :: Error :: Ok ) { return scale ; // RangeMismatch (x2 or /2) or ScaleMismatch (reference): do not publish } out = bank . value ; return ads7952 :: Error :: Ok ; } After a RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch , do not publish the bank. Restart with Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() : the reset and the start-up check run again. A failed CheckScale() leaves the driver uninitialised by itself.
docs.title: Proving the scale: the scale monitor

docs.text: A ratiometric sensor (for example a bridge or an amplified pressure sensor rated "10 % to 90 % of supply") outputs a fraction of its own supply . The ADC measures volts against VREF. Decoding the sensor against the ADC's full scale, or against a nominal 5.0 V, is only right while the sensor's supply is exactly that value. A supply that sags to 4.45 V while the decoder assumes 5.0 V under-reads every span by 11 % (4.45 / 5.0 = 0.89). Measure the sensor's supply on another channel of the same scan and divide: // A ratiometric sensor (output = a fraction of its own supply) read on channel 3, its supply // measured on channel 9 through a divider of exactly 1/2. Both conversions come from one bank, so // the reference and the range cancel: the result does not depend on VREF or on the 5 V rail. uint32_t SensorFractionPpm ( const ads7952 :: ADS7952 < MyPort >& adc , const ads7952 :: Bank & bank ) { const uint64_t signal_uv = adc . ToMicrovolts ( bank , 3 ); const uint64_t supply_uv = 2U * static_cast < uint64_t > ( adc . ToMicrovolts ( bank , 9 )); if ( supply_uv == 0U ) { return 0U ; // no supply: the caller treats the sensor as absent } return static_cast < uint32_t > (( signal_uv * 1000000U ) / supply_uv ); // 100000 = 10 % of supply } Choice Effect Supply measured in the same bank Reference and range cancel; supply ripple between the two conversions does not Divider for the supply channel Must keep the supply's channel inside the range: ½ puts a 5 V supply at 2.5 V No supply measurement The result is only as good as the rail's tolerance: say so where the value is used

docs.text: From sections 8.3.1, 9.1.1, 10 and 11 of the datasheet: Item Requirement +VA 2.7 V to 5.25 V, well regulated; 1 µF ceramic at each +VA pin, as close as possible +VBD 1.7 V to +VA (never above +VA); 1 µF ceramic at the pin REFP An external low-noise reference (the datasheet names the REF5025, a 2.5 V band-gap); 10 µF ceramic from REFP to REFM, directly next to the pins, its ground routed to REFM by a short trace Characterised reference The electrical tables are measured at VREF = 2.5 V ± 0.1 V; section 8.3.1 asks for 2.5 V ± 10 mV; the chip operates from 2.0 V to 3.0 V Grounds A copper fill under the chip ties AGND, BDGND, AINM and REFM, with at least four vias to the analog ground plane Vias None between a decoupling capacitor and its pin Analog inputs With MXO tied to AINP, a source impedance of 50 Ω or less; a buffer between MXO and AINP relaxes it (Figure 61) Digital lines Kept apart from the analog inputs: the input bandwidth makes the chip sensitive to digital edges Inputs -0.3 V to +VA + 0.3 V, absolute (section 7.1) Design guidance that is not in the datasheet, to confirm on your bench: A resistor divider for the monitor or a supply channel has a high source impedance. Put a capacitor from the channel to AGND (for example 100 nF) so that the sample charge comes from it, and check that the reading does not move with the SCLK rate or the position of the channel in the sequence. Measure +VA at the chip under full load (the sensors on, motors and other loads running) before choosing the range. The value to declare is the lowest you saw, less the regulator's tolerance.

docs.text: Repository setup ¶ The one-time steps an org owner runs after creating a repository from the template, and before the first PR. The scripts are in kokeb-labs/.github/org/ . Each one is a dry run unless given --apply , and --repo limits it to one repository. The rules behind them are in repo-governance.md . 1. Create and scaffold ¶ gh repo create kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-<chip> --public --template kokeb-labs/driver-template --clone cd driver-<chip> git switch -c feat/initial-driver python3 tools/setup.py tools/setup.py asks for the bus and a one-sentence description, scaffolds, builds and runs the host tests; tools/scaffold.py --help lists every option ( --platforms host,esp32 is a driver's default; a library gets host unless esp32 is asked for); it ends with a checklist of what is left to fill in. 2. Apply the org settings ¶ From a checkout of kokeb-labs/.github , after adding the repository to org/repos.json by PR (its entry sets the About: description and topics): python3 org/kokeb_org.py --repo driver-ads7952 # the plan: every setting that would change python3 org/kokeb_org.py --repo driver-ads7952 --apply # settings, security, Actions, rulesets, labels Run it without --apply first to see what changes. 3. docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host tests against a model of the chip, a fuzzer that corrupts what the chip sends back, compiled documentation, an install test, ESP32 and Cortex-M builds, static analysis and measured quality gates, on every pull request. Host tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a protocol model of the chip ( tests/mock_ads7952.hpp ) that runs it frame by frame: the sample taken at each CS falling edge of the channel acquired in the frame before, the multiplexer switching as Manual, Auto-1 and Auto-2 say, the range that applies to each acquisition, DI11 gating the mode word, "continue" words, the GPIO register with its reset in the next frame, the two-frame Auto-1 program, the Auto-2 program that restarts the sequence, the alarm sequence with its exit frame, the alarm and GPIO pins, power-down and wake-up, the invalid first conversion and the power-up time. The faults are the bus and board conditions a broken or floating line produces, and the ones the datasheet names: MISO floating high, stuck low, a fixed word (0x0E83), MOSI echoed or noise; SDI not reaching the chip; a brown-out that resets every register, poked by a test or on its own before a chosen frame, with the conversion in flight kept or lost; a GPIO pin held by the board; failed transfers (before and after the chip took the frame), lost and replaced transfers. They build with the firmware's flags, -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti , and warnings as errors, on GCC and Clang. ads7952_host_tests runs 81 test cases; with the Kconfig, version, install, Doxygen, host-example, compile-fail and fuzz-corpus tests CTest runs 21 tests. cmake -S . -B build -DADS7952_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_ads7952.cpp The lifecycle (no I/O before the start, the reset and the frames of the start, a retried start, a chip left inside a program sequence, restart from power-down), Validate() , the identity check against every bus fault and on every variant, Manual reads and their frame counts, pipelined lists, Auto-1 and Auto-2 scans (entry, the running sequence, a pass starting anywhere, a lost mask, a brown-out), SetRange() and the skipped reply, program registers with and without Verify::ReadBack , alarms and alarm pins, GPIOs and their read-back, ApplyConfig() before and after the start, logging tests/test_bus_faults.cpp Every frame of every operation, EnsureInitialized() included, fails in turn, before and after the chip took it; each returns Bus and the next read works; every frame of a read is lost in turn and none yields another channel's result; the repairs after a failed mask or alarm frame tests/fuzz/ The fuzz target; CTest replays its corpus ( ads7952_fuzz_ads7952_corpus ), see below tests/test_errors.cpp Every chip-specific value (16 to 22) and Unsupported are returned by a real call tests/test_reset.cpp A reset the chip does on its own mid-session ( brownout_before_frame , with the conversion in flight kept or lost): the model reloads the reset values and gives one invalid result; DeviceReset from a read, a select, a list, an Auto-1 scan and CheckScale() ; the driver uninitialised after every mismatch; ApplyConfig() writing every register on every part; the GPIO0 alarm re-armed tests/test_version.cpp The version getters follow the generated header (also against a 9.8.7 probe) tests/test_kconfig.cpp KconfigDefaults() with and without CONFIG_ values tests/compile_fail/ Code that must not compile, each for its EXPECT: diagnostic: a port without DelayUs() , a void Transfer() , a Transfer() with a narrowed length or without noexcept , a DelayUs(uint16_t) , a Log() without noexcept , a class that is not a port tests/mock_ads7952.hpp The chip model, with its own frame format; the mock ports over it are in mock_ads7952_bus.hpp tests/test_model.cpp The model's frame format, reset values, channel counts and timing against the driver's, with static_assert tests/check_version_copy.cmake _config/Doxyfile carries the CMake version examples/host/ The host example, built with the test flags and run ( ads7952_host_example ) tests/check_install.cmake Installs into a scratch prefix and builds tests/install_consumer/ with find_package(ads7952) tests/check_doxygen.cmake Doxygen with _config/Doxyfile and warnings as errors, when doxygen is installed The model does not reproduce the chip's analog or electrical behaviour, and two points the datasheet leaves open are modelled the conservative way: see Status and limitations . The model stands alone ¶ tests/mock_ads7952.hpp is written from the datasheet, not from the driver: it does not include ads7952_registers.hpp or ads7952_types.hpp . Its command codes, bit positions, reset values, channel counts and power-up time are its own (namespace ads7952_test::chip , each with the datasheet section), so a wrong constant in the driver cannot hide behind the same wrong constant in the model (handbook KB-TST-030). tests/test_model.cpp compares the two at compile time: // Command words, DI15:12 (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 11, 13). static_assert ( chip :: kCommandShift == reg :: kCommandShift && chip :: kContinue == reg :: kContinue && chip :: kManual == reg :: kManual && chip :: kAuto1 == reg :: kAuto1 && chip :: kAuto2 == reg :: kAuto2 && chip :: kGpioProgram == reg :: kGpioProgram && chip :: kAuto1Program == reg :: kAuto1Program && chip :: kAuto2Program == reg :: kAuto2Program && chip :: kAlarmProgramGroup0 == reg :: kAlarmProgramGroup0 ); // Mode control word (Tables 1, 2, 5). static_assert ( chip :: kProgramEnable == reg :: kProgramEnable && chip :: kAutoReset == reg :: kAutoReset && chip :: kManualChannelShift == reg :: kManualChannelShift && chip :: kRangeTwoVref == reg :: kRangeTwoVref && chip :: kPowerDown == reg :: kPowerDown && chip :: kGpioReadout == reg :: kGpioReadout && chip :: kGpioDataMask == reg :: kGpioDataMask ); // Program registers (Tables 6, 11, 13) and their reset values (section 8.5.3). static_assert ( chip :: kAuto2LastShift == reg :: kAuto2LastShift && chip :: kGpioResetAll == reg :: kGpioResetAll && chip :: kGpio3PowerDown == reg :: kGpio3PowerDown && chip :: kGpio2Range == reg :: kGpio2Range && chip :: kGpioAlarmShift == reg :: kGpioAlarmShift ); static_assert ( chip :: kAlarmChannelShift == reg :: kAlarmChannelShift && chip :: kAlarmHigh == reg :: kAlarmHigh && chip :: kAlarmExit == reg :: kAlarmExit && chip :: kAlarmThresholdMask == reg :: kAlarmThresholdMask && chip :: kAlarmHighReset == reg :: kAlarmHighReset && chip :: kAlarmLowReset == reg :: kAlarmLowReset ); // Reply word and frame (section 8.1), timing (section 7.6). static_assert ( chip :: kReplyAddressShift == reg :: kReplyAddressShift && chip :: kReplyCodeMask == reg :: kReplyCodeMask && chip :: kFrameBytes == ads7952 :: kFrameBytes && chip :: kPowerUpUs == ads7952 :: kPowerUpUs ); // Parts, packages and channel counts (Table 4, section 8.5.2). static_assert ( chip :: ChannelCount ( chip :: Part :: Ads7950 ) == ads7952 :: ChannelCount ( Variant :: Ads7950 ) && chip :: ChannelCount ( chip :: Part :: Ads7951 ) == ads7952 :: ChannelCount ( Variant :: Ads7951 ) && chip :: ChannelCount ( chip :: Part :: Ads7952 ) == ads7952 :: ChannelCount ( Variant :: Ads7952 ) && chip :: ChannelCount ( chip :: Part :: Ads7953 ) == ads7952 :: ChannelCount ( Variant :: Ads7953 )); static_assert ( ads7952_test :: ModelPart ( Variant :: Ads7953 ) == chip :: Part :: Ads7953 && ads7952_test :: DriverVariant ( chip :: Part :: Ads7950 ) == Variant :: Ads7950 ); static_assert ( ads7952_test :: ModelPackage ( Package :: Vqfn ) == chip :: Package :: Vqfn && ads7952_test :: DriverPackage ( chip :: Package :: Tssop ) == Package :: Tssop ); When the build stops on one of these, one of the two is wrong: check it against the section the model names, and fix that one. Every behaviour found on hardware becomes a fault mode of the model and a test that fails on the code before the fix; the model's virtual clock is Elapse() , driven by the mock port's DelayUs() . Strict dialect ¶ Every target builds as ISO C++20 ( CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF , -pedantic-errors , the C++20 deprecations as errors), and the target ads7952_header_checks compiles each public header alone and asserts __cplusplus == 202002L (handbook KB-CPP20-001). It builds with the host tests on GCC and Clang and with the Cortex-M cross-build; examples/esp32/main/ads7952_cxx20_check.cpp does the same inside the ESP-IDF build, which otherwise compiles C++ in a newer GNU dialect. The tests and fuzzers build with the standard library's assertions ( _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS , libc++ hardening), so an out-of-range span access traps. Fuzz tests ¶ Everything the driver receives comes from MISO, so MISO is what a noisy cable, an unplugged board or a broken chip controls. tests/fuzz/fuzz_ads7952.cpp lets libFuzzer choose the part, the package and a configuration (sometimes for another part, sometimes invalid), then up to 64 driver calls, and on every transfer what the bus does: pass the model's reply, fail the transfer, lose it (the chip never sees it, MISO floats), flip bits of the reply or replace it. Between calls it changes the board: MISO floating, stuck low, a fixed word, echoing or noisy, SDI not reaching the chip, a brown-out, the analog inputs, the GPIO inputs, a pin held low. After every call the target checks the driver's promises and aborts, naming the line, when one breaks: a failed call returns an Error the enum defines (never one documented as not returned) and T{} ; every transfer is one 2-byte frame with both buffers; before EnsureInitialized() no call makes a transfer, and InvalidArgument means nothing was sent; EnsureInitialized() never returns Ok on a dead bus (MISO floating, stuck, a fixed word, an echo, or a deaf chip) unless a transfer of the call was tampered; a conversion never returns another channel's result : without a tampered or untrusted transfer in the call, every code it returns is one the chip sent for that channel in that call; while the bus has been clean since the start, every code is the chip's conversion of that channel in the configured range, and the chip's program registers and range are what the driver was told. after DeviceReset , ChannelMismatch or SequenceMismatch the driver is uninitialised. The fuzzer found two bugs, both fixed with a unit test and a regress-* input each: A failed alarm frame, then a failed repair frame, left the chip inside the alarm sequence; the next EnsureInitialized() 's reset word was taken as a threshold, so the start went ahead without a reset. Every start now opens with two frames that end any program sequence ( regress-reset-eaten-by-alarm-sequence ). A chip whose SDI broke while it ran an Auto-1 sequence of exactly the two identity channels answered the identity check's two selects in turn and passed it. The check now asks for the first address twice, which no deaf chip can answer ( regress-deaf-chip-scanning-identity-pair ). The bus-fault sweep found a third before the fuzzer ran: a chip that saw the Auto-1 request but not the mask took the next Manual word as its mask. docs.text: The tests build the real driver against a protocol model of the chip ( tests/mock_ads7952.hpp ) that runs it frame by frame: the sample taken at each CS falling edge of the channel acquired in the frame before, the multiplexer switching as Manual, Auto-1 and Auto-2 say, the range that applies to each acquisition, DI11 gating the mode word, "continue" words, the GPIO register with its reset in the next frame, the two-frame Auto-1 program, the Auto-2 program that restarts the sequence, the alarm sequence with its exit frame, the alarm and GPIO pins, power-down and wake-up, the invalid first conversion and the power-up time. The faults are the bus and board conditions a broken or floating line produces, and the ones the datasheet names: MISO floating high, stuck low, a fixed word (0x0E83), MOSI echoed or noise; SDI not reaching the chip; a brown-out that resets every register, poked by a test or on its own before a chosen frame, with the conversion in flight kept or lost; a GPIO pin held by the board; failed transfers (before and after the chip took the frame), lost and replaced transfers. docs.text: Everything the driver receives comes from MISO, so MISO is what a noisy cable, an unplugged board or a broken chip controls. tests/fuzz/fuzz_ads7952.cpp lets libFuzzer choose the part, the package and a configuration (sometimes for another part, sometimes invalid), then up to 64 driver calls, and on every transfer what the bus does: pass the model's reply, fail the transfer, lose it (the chip never sees it, MISO floats), flip bits of the reply or replace it. docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms, causes and fixes, cheapest check first. GetLastReply() holds the last reply word the driver received; log it with the error. TraceFrames() shows the raw replies of a manual select, the bench's first tool. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Texas Instruments SLAS605 C: Power-up and the programming sequence: 8.4.3 Device Power-Up Sequence, Figure 49, p. 30 Manual mode and the two-frame read latency: 8.4.4 Operating in Manual Mode, Figures 50 and 51, Table 1, p. 31 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . EnsureInitialized returns Bus ¶ The port reported a failure: either EnsureInitialized() returned false or a transfer did. Check that your port's EnsureInitialized() returns true on its own (log it). Check the bus pins in your port against the board. With a logic analyser, check that the first frames (0x1000, 0x0000, then the reset word 0x4200) appear on the bus, each with its own CS pulse. EnsureInitialized returns NoDevice ¶ Every identity reply read 0xFFFF: nothing drives MISO. The board is unplugged or unpowered, CS does not reach the chip, or SDO is open with a pull-up. Check +VA and +VBD, CS and SDO continuity. EnsureInitialized returns DeviceIdMismatch ¶ The replies did not carry the channel addresses the driver selected. Look at GetLastReply() , or run the identity by hand with TraceFrames() after a temporary start: Replies Likely cause Fix 0x0000 every time MISO stuck or floating low Check SDO continuity and what else drives MISO Address 0 every time, codes that vary The chip never receives SDI: it stays in Manual mode on channel 0, its reset state, and all-zero SDI words continue it (sections 8.4.1, 8.4.7) Check SDI (MOSI) continuity, the SPI mode and +VBD One fixed word (for example 0x0E83) MISO carries a pattern, not the chip Unpowered board, or another device on MISO 0xFFxx MOSI echoed on MISO SDI shorted to SDO Addresses one frame late or early CS does not toggle between frames, or the port bursts frames One transfer per frame, CS high between them Addresses with a shifted bit Wrong SPI mode Mode 0 Reads or scans return DeviceReset ¶ A reply came from channel 0, the channel the chip powers up on (section 8.4.3), where the driver expected another: the chip was reset behind the driver's back, most often by a supply dip under a large load. Its registers are back at their reset values: Range 1, no GPIO function (the alarm outputs are off), the reset alarm thresholds and sequences. The driver is uninitialised and every call returns NotInitialized : call EnsureInitialized() , which resets and programs the chip again and checks it. If it recurs, check +VA and its decoupling under load (section 10). A reply from channel 0 has two other causes that look the same, so the restart also checks the bus: MISO stuck low after the start: every reply reads 0x0000, channel 0. EnsureInitialized() then returns DeviceIdMismatch ; check the MISO line and the chip's supply. A lost select from channel 0 : the chip stays on channel 0 when a select of another channel does not reach it (noise on SDI or CS). It is rare; EnsureInitialized() succeeds and the driver goes on. Reads return ChannelMismatch ¶ A Manual reply carried another address than the channel read: a lost frame, noise on the bus, or a chip that stopped following the selects (SDI lost after the start). The driver is uninitialised (it cannot rule out a reset): call EnsureInitialized() . If the start fails with DeviceIdMismatch , check SDI. Scans return SequenceMismatch ¶ An Auto-1 or Auto-2 pass was not one turn of the sequence: a frame was lost or the chip left the mode. The driver is uninitialised: call EnsureInitialized() , which writes the sequence again. Another master sending frames to the chip (a DMA stream with the wrong word) shows here too. Codes are all about the same, or twice what they should be ¶ All codes equal, VREF_MON included : the chip is not converting the channels you think. Run TraceFrames() and check the address nibble follows the select. Codes doubled, a 2.5 V reference reading 4095 : the chip runs Range 1 where you expect Range 2. A reset behind the driver's back does this (a brown-out); the next read or Auto entry sends the range again, and a restart writes everything. While the driver reads channel 0 alone, the reset shows in no reply: see Status and limitations . A GPIO2 left as the range input ignores DI06: EnsureInitialized() resets it. With Config::monitor declared this is RangeMismatch , not a wrong value. Codes halved : the opposite, Range 2 where you expect Range 1. The first channel of a scan reads mid-scale : a reply taken from the frame before the result. The driver never returns those; check code that decodes raw frames by position instead of by address. SetGpioOutputs returns WriteMismatch ¶ With Verify::ReadBack , a pin did not read back the level written. The board holds the pin (a short, a strong pull, another driver on the net), or the pin is not an output in Config::gpio.output_mask . RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch ¶ The scale monitor ( Config::monitor ) is out of its window. RangeMismatch : the code is what the other range gives; the chip converts in the other range. With GPIO2 as the range input, the pin is at the other level from Config::range ; otherwise the chip was reset after the range was sent ( CheckScale() then returns DeviceReset ). After a failed CheckScale() the driver is uninitialised. ScaleMismatch : neither range explains the code; REFP is missing or still settling after power-up, or the monitor channel does not carry the declared voltage. Read the channel with TraceFrames() to see its code. See Reference, range and supplies . SetRange returns Unsupported ¶ Config::gpio.gpio2_range_input is set: the GPIO2 pin selects the range and the chip ignores DI06. Drive the pin, or clear the option. EnsureInitialized returns Unsupported ¶ The Config asks for GPIO1, GPIO2 or GPIO3 on the VQFN package, which brings out GPIO0 only.

Look at GetLastReply() , or run the identity by hand with TraceFrames() after a temporary start: Replies Likely cause Fix 0x0000 every time MISO stuck or floating low Check SDO continuity and what else drives MISO Address 0 every time, codes that vary The chip never receives SDI: it stays in Manual mode on channel 0, its reset state, and all-zero SDI words continue it (sections 8.4.1, 8.4.7) Check SDI (MOSI) continuity, the SPI mode and +VBD One fixed word (for example 0x0E83) MISO carries a pattern, not the chip Unpowered board, or another device on MISO 0xFFxx MOSI echoed on MISO SDI shorted to SDO Addresses one frame late or early CS does not toggle between frames, or the port bursts frames One transfer per frame, CS high between them Addresses with a shifted bit Wrong SPI mode Mode 0
docs.title: EnsureInitialized returns DeviceIdMismatch

docs.text: A reply came from channel 0, the channel the chip powers up on (section 8.4.3), where the driver expected another: the chip was reset behind the driver's back, most often by a supply dip under a large load. Its registers are back at their reset values: Range 1, no GPIO function (the alarm outputs are off), the reset alarm thresholds and sequences. The driver is uninitialised and every call returns NotInitialized : call EnsureInitialized() , which resets and programs the chip again and checks it. If it recurs, check +VA and its decoupling under load (section 10). A reply from channel 0 has two other causes that look the same, so the restart also checks the bus: MISO stuck low after the start: every reply reads 0x0000, channel 0. EnsureInitialized() then returns DeviceIdMismatch ; check the MISO line and the chip's supply. A lost select from channel 0 : the chip stays on channel 0 when a select of another channel does not reach it (noise on SDI or CS). It is rare; EnsureInitialized() succeeds and the driver goes on.
docs.title: Reads or scans return DeviceReset

docs.text: A Manual reply carried another address than the channel read: a lost frame, noise on the bus, or a chip that stopped following the selects (SDI lost after the start). The driver is uninitialised (it cannot rule out a reset): call EnsureInitialized() . If the start fails with DeviceIdMismatch , check SDI.
docs.title: Reads return ChannelMismatch

docs.text: An Auto-1 or Auto-2 pass was not one turn of the sequence: a frame was lost or the chip left the mode. The driver is uninitialised: call EnsureInitialized() , which writes the sequence again. Another master sending frames to the chip (a DMA stream with the wrong word) shows here too.
docs.title: Scans return SequenceMismatch

docs.text: All codes equal, VREF_MON included : the chip is not converting the channels you think. Run TraceFrames() and check the address nibble follows the select. Codes doubled, a 2.5 V reference reading 4095 : the chip runs Range 1 where you expect Range 2. A reset behind the driver's back does this (a brown-out); the next read or Auto entry sends the range again, and a restart writes everything. While the driver reads channel 0 alone, the reset shows in no reply: see Status and limitations . A GPIO2 left as the range input ignores DI06: EnsureInitialized() resets it. With Config::monitor declared this is RangeMismatch , not a wrong value. Codes halved : the opposite, Range 2 where you expect Range 1. The first channel of a scan reads mid-scale : a reply taken from the frame before the result. The driver never returns those; check code that decodes raw frames by position instead of by address.
docs.title: Codes are all about the same, or twice what they should be

docs.text: With Verify::ReadBack , a pin did not read back the level written. The board holds the pin (a short, a strong pull, another driver on the net), or the pin is not an output in Config::gpio.output_mask .
docs.title: SetGpioOutputs returns WriteMismatch

docs.text: The scale monitor ( Config::monitor ) is out of its window. RangeMismatch : the code is what the other range gives; the chip converts in the other range. With GPIO2 as the range input, the pin is at the other level from Config::range ; otherwise the chip was reset after the range was sent ( CheckScale() then returns DeviceReset ). After a failed CheckScale() the driver is uninitialised. ScaleMismatch : neither range explains the code; REFP is missing or still settling after power-up, or the monitor channel does not carry the declared voltage. Read the channel with TraceFrames() to see its code. See Reference, range and supplies .
docs.title: RangeMismatch or ScaleMismatch

docs.text: Config::gpio.gpio2_range_input is set: the GPIO2 pin selects the range and the chip ignores DI06. Drive the pin, or clear the option.
docs.title: SetRange returns Unsupported

docs.text: The Config asks for GPIO1, GPIO2 or GPIO3 on the VQFN package, which brings out GPIO0 only.
docs.title: EnsureInitialized returns Unsupported

In each panel the top row is the word the driver sends on SDI, the middle row the channel the multiplexer acquires during that frame, and the bottom row the reply on SDO: the conversion of the channel acquired in the frame before, sampled at this frame's CS falling edge, tagged with its address in DO15:12. In Auto-1 (bottom), entering the mode restarts the sequence at its first channel: with channels 2, 5 and 6 programmed, the first result arrives two frames after the Auto-1 word, and from then on every Auto-1 word without restart (DI11 = 1, the range again) returns the next channel of the sequence, so a pass costs one frame per channel.
